title: Scalp-electrode acoustoelectric imaging needs hours to weeks of maximal cortical activity per 4-mm voxel under a 2 K heating limit in a human head model; implanted contacts need seconds to minutes
abstract: Transcranial acoustoelectric brain imaging (tABI) cannot detect normal human cortical currents through scalp electrodes in a practical time when the ultrasound stays inside heating limits. This matters because several groups develop tABI as a non-invasive method with millimetre and millisecond resolution and state that it is within range of strong neural currents. In tABI, focused ultrasound changes tissue resistivity by a fraction K times the pressure, and electrodes record the neural current of the focus as sidebands of the ultrasound frequency. With the reciprocity theorem we show that the tABI signal equals K times the pressure times the ordinary EEG voltage of the tissue inside the focus, times a laminar factor of at most 1. Because the signal is linear in pressure and the noise is white, no ultrasound waveform can shorten the detection time at a fixed time-averaged intensity. We calculated the signal for the adult head with the New York Head lead field (231 scalp electrodes, 74,382 cortical sites), a validated layered-head solver, a steady-state skull-heating model, the first measured K for brain (0.022 %/MPa) and the measured maximum dipole-moment density of cortex (about 1 nAm/mm2). For a voxel 4.3 mm wide, the best design inside the critical angle of skull bone is 0.435 MHz with F-number 0.87. A 2 K temperature rise then allows a focal intensity of only 21 to 260 mW/cm2 (median 74) for cortex 16 mm deep, and the signal is about 0.045 nV. With nominal values and maximal activity, the median gyral-crown site needs 15 h per voxel with all 231 electrodes; over the whole cortex, with the beam tilted at most 20 degrees, the median is 20 days, and with a stricter tilt model two thirds of the cortex cannot be reached. Only when K, the laminar factor, electrode noise, skull window, site, lead-field model and beam angle all take their best values does the time fall to about 1 min. Implanted contacts have 30 to 100 times larger lead fields: a subdural ECoG contact needs 30 s and a depth contact 2 mm away needs 100 s. Published phantom thresholds are 360 to 11,000 times above the physiological signal on the scalp, and the cited seizure current densities (1 to 10 mA/cm2) are 10 to 250 times above the measured maximum. Limits: planar models for implanted electrodes and heating, model-dependent beam-tilt loss, no in vivo K, laminar factor or scalp-electrode noise near 0.4 MHz, and sustained activity assumed.
